newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, key data awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, key data awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended marginally lower on Friday after a narrow-ranged trading session in which many players were sidelined, waiting for several influential economic reports that are due next week.
"It was only a 9/32 point trading range (on the 30-year bond)," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "The market was extremely quiet."
The Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond ended at 93-21/32 on Friday, down 4/32.
Two-year notes edged down 1/32 to 99-22/32, their yields closing at 6.54 percent.
Economic reports released on Friday proved to be market non-events, analysts said.

The National Association of Realtors reported that sales of existing U.S. homes fell 2.8 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.11 million. Wall Street economists had forecast March sales of 4.14 million units.
At the same time the Commerce Department reported revisions to January and February trade figures to reflect corrected oil import data.
"The existing homes report and trade revisions were non-events," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "Everyone is looking at next week's data."
Next week brings a powerful group of economic data.

The Employment Cost Index (ECI), which has drawn heightened market attention since Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan mentioned it in his July 1996 Humphrey-Hawkins Congressional testimony, is due on Tuesday and, according to a Reuters poll of economists, is expected to be up 0.9 percent in the first quarter after rising 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.

GDP data, due on Wednesday, are expected to show that the U.S. economy grew 4.1 percent in the first quarter. And Labor Department data on Friday are likely to reflect a 5.2 percent unemployment rate, payroll expansion of 211,000 jobs and a 0.3 percent rise in hourly earnings, economists told Reuters.
"That's a lot of very important data and we expect that it will still show signs of a vibrant, robust economy and possibly hints of rising wage pressures," said Youngdahl.
Rupkey said the market "showed its true colors" this week.
"We've gone down again," he said. "It makes people believe ... we are in a bear market and they're short out there."

Rupkey said people "are alarmed" about the Employment Cost Index (ECI), though he noted that the market has rallied a point in fast trading immediately after each of the last three ECI reports -- on July 30, October 29 and January 28.

New supply continued to weigh on the market on Friday, analysts said. The Treasury sold one-, two- and five-year notes earlier this week and participants said dealers had to cut prices to entice buyers to take the paper off their hands.
"There was a little maldistribution," said Youngdahl. "Friday still saw some backing and filling after the auctions and caution ahead of next week's data."

Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the market kept an eye on budget talks in Washington and added that the bond market "wasn't getting very much support from Fed officials lately."

Indeed, Richmond Fed Bank President Alfred Broaddus told a banking organization on Friday afternoon that the U.S. economic picture was "really bright," a remark that would not stop the market from expecting another Fed rate hike in May.
On Friday, three-month bill rates rose one basis point to 5.16 percent. Six-month bill rates rose two basis points to 5.40 percent. Year bill rates rose one basis point to 5.74 percent.
Five-year notes fell 1/32 to 99-4/32, yielding 6.84 percent.
The 6-1/4 percent 10-year notes ended down 1/32 to 95-5/32, yielding 6.94 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
